catalog_quote: Stress has been posited for Isthmus Zapotec; it affects the length of the vowel itself (before lenis consonants), or the length of the consonant that follows (if it is fortis), or the tone (see Conventions). It usually falls on the penultimate (or the only) syllable of the root when the vowels are modal, although there are exceptions. Convincing examples clearly showing that the generalization is not appropriately stated as referring to the first syllable of the root are not easy to come by since stems longer than two syllables often seem to be compounds or to derive from compounds. The word /wakaaba/ ... ‘a particularly venomous tarantula’ may be an appropriate example. The weight of a syllable also affects the placement of stress. sweep_summary: One sweep item, Pickett 1951 (WORD 7: 60-65), the article previously marked 'cited in the JIPA references; not opened' and 'Cloudflare-blocked'. The publisher copy is still blocked from our machine, but the Internet Archive Serials-in-Microfilm scan of WORD 7(1) (sim_word_1951-04_7_1, unrestricted, text layer) was fetched sources; the whole issue, its scanned text, and an extracted six-page PDF plus text of the article are and logged in and md5sums recorded). Read in full: stress is predictable over the grammatical word, falling on the unique heavy (complex-nucleus) syllable in any position, else on the penult; short vowel + fortis consonant counts as heavy (VV); tone is irrelevant; loans get penult or last-closed-syllable stress. Bears on the catalog: REFINES the 'weight-hedged' coding (deciding source JIPA 2010 by the same Pickett with Marlett): it supplies the explicit weight algorithm behind JIPA's hedge and agrees with all of JIPA's clauses, so the coding stands; the catalog's source note should change from 'not opened' to read, and Pickett 1951 should be cited as the primary support for the weight clause. It does not supersede JIPA 2010 as the deciding source (later, same author, adds root-domain and clitic facts). Still unread for this language and outside this sweep's items: Mock 1988 (doi:10.1515/9783110874266.197, paywalled) and Marlett & Pickett 1987 (doi:10.1086/466066, paywalled). all discovery here was via Crossref, Unpaywall and the archive.org search API.

new_statements.quote: Stress falls (1) on the syllable containing a complex nucleus in words with one and only one such syllable, (2) on the penultimate syllable (a) in words containing two or more syllables each with complex nucleus and (b) in words containing only open syllables each with simple nucleus, (3) on the last closed syllable of words with no syllable of complex nucleus but with one or more closed syllables. Thus we conclude that for both words of native origin and loan words, stress is predictable in Isthmus Zapotec.
new_statements.citation: Pickett, Velma B. 1951. Nonphonemic stress: a problem in stress placement in Isthmus Zapotec. WORD 7(1): 60-65. doi:10.1080/00437956.1951.11659392
new_statements.locator: p. 65, the italicised 'combination statement' and the following conclusion (PDF p. 6 of the extracted file = scan page 69 of); supporting: p. 61 tentative rule and fn. 5 (nucleus types), pp. 62-64 (short V + fortis C = VV)
new_statements.reading: A categorical, weight-driven rule over the grammatical word: the single heavy syllable (long vowel, glottalised nucleus, or short vowel + fortis consonant reanalysed as VV) is stressed in whatever position it occupies; with two or more heavy syllables, or (loans only) no heavy syllable, stress defaults to the penult; loans with no heavy syllable but a closed syllable stress the last closed syllable. Tone is irrelevant; prefixes are not mentioned as stress-bearing (all examples with prefixes stress the root). This is the explicit algorithm behind the JIPA 2010 hedge ('usually penultimate of the root... weight also affects placement... final diphthongs/laryngealized vowels attract stress'): it agrees with every JIPA clause and adds that the weight attraction is general (any position, not only final) and exceptionless in the 1944-50 data. It supports, and if anything strengthens, the 'weight' half of the current 'weight-hedged' coding; the hedge itself is JIPA's own 'usually/exceptions', which Pickett 1951 does not share.

sources.note: Read in full (six pages, text layer, checked against the page image). Stress is fully predictable ('nonphonemic') over the grammatical word: it falls on the unique heavy ('complex-nucleus') syllable wherever it is (initial 'toobi 'one', final kana'zaa 'is walking around', nan'daaʔ 'bitter', gi'raaʔ 'all'); when a word has two or more heavy syllables it falls on the penult ('šoonoó 'eight', 'biʔkuʔ 'dog'); tone plays no role (p. 60).
